title: Coding Interview Patterns
tagline: Seven battle-tested algorithmic patterns — two pointers, sliding window, fast/slow, merge intervals, prefix sum, BFS/DFS, and backtracking — and the recognition signals that tell you which one to reach for.

sections.content:
Coding interviews look intimidating until you realize they are testing a surprisingly small vocabulary of recurring ideas. Most LeetCode-style problems, regardless of their surface story — rearranging characters, scheduling meetings, counting islands, generating parentheses — reduce to one of seven fundamental algorithmic patterns. Once you can **recognize which pattern applies**, the solution almost writes itself.

The seven patterns are: **Two Pointers**, which collapses O(n²) pair searches into O(n) by marching indices toward each other from opposite ends of a sorted array. **Sliding Window**, which tracks a contiguous subrange without rescanning from scratch, handling substring and subarray problems in linear time. **Fast/Slow Pointers** (Floyd's algorithm), which detects cycles and finds midpoints in linked lists using only two integer-sized state variables. **Merge Intervals**, which tames overlapping ranges by sorting once and then sweeping through a single pass. **Prefix Sum**, which answers arbitrary range-sum queries in O(1) after O(n) preprocessing, and counts subarrays with a target sum in O(n) via a hash-map companion. **Breadth-First Search** and **Depth-First Search**, the two canonical graph traversals that underpin shortest paths, connected components, topological ordering, and tree problems. And finally **Backtracking**, the systematic, pruned enumeration that generates all subsets, permutations, and valid board placements.

This chapter goes deep on each pattern: what it is, why it works mathematically, where it falls short, and how to build a clean implementation from a mental template. You will also learn the **recognition signals** — specific phrases and structural clues in a problem statement that serve as a reliable trigger. After reading this chapter and practicing thirty to forty problems with these patterns explicitly in mind, you will spend far less interview time wondering what to do and far more time executing cleanly.

sections.caption: Pattern decision tree — each branch maps a recognition signal in the problem statement to its canonical algorithm family.

sections.title: Patterns as Lenses
sections.content:
Think of each pattern as a **lens** that reframes the problem. A word problem about finding the longest substring with at most two distinct characters looks genuinely hard without a lens. Slide the *Sliding Window* lens in front of it and you see a window expanding rightward and shrinking leftward — a mechanical process any engineer can implement in five minutes.

**Two Pointers** is like two people walking toward each other along a sorted row of lockers, searching for a pair whose combined numbers hit a target. If the current pair is too large, the right person steps left; too small, the left person steps right. They never need to visit every pair — O(n) steps total, zero wasted work.

**Fast/Slow Pointers** mimics the classic tortoise-and-hare race: on a circular track, a hare running at twice the tortoise's speed will always lap the tortoise and catch up to it. If there is no loop, the hare simply falls off the end. One invariant, zero extra memory.

**Backtracking** is a maze explorer who annotates every dead end and returns to the last intersection to try a different branch. Unlike brute force, it prunes entire subtrees the moment it knows they cannot lead to a valid answer — turning an exponential search space into something tractable in practice.

The key skill is not memorizing solutions — it is training the pattern-recognition reflex so that reading a problem statement triggers the right lens automatically.

sections.title: Pattern 1: Two Pointers
sections.content:
**What it is.** Two Pointers maintains two indices into an array (or string) and moves them according to a comparison, converging until they meet or cross. The pattern exploits **sorted order** or **symmetry** to eliminate the need to check every pair.

**Recognition signals.** The problem involves: a sorted array; finding a pair or triplet that sums to a target; removing duplicates or elements in-place; checking if a string is a palindrome; or partitioning an array around a pivot (as in Dutch National Flag).

**Why it works.** In a sorted array, if `arr[left] + arr[right] > target`, then `arr[left] + arr[right-1]` and every pair with the same `right` is guaranteed too large (since `arr[right-1] < arr[right]`). So decrementing `right` is always safe. The symmetric argument applies when the sum is too small — increment `left`. Every step eliminates at least one index from contention, so the total work is O(n).

**Complexity.** O(n) time, O(1) extra space. For three-sum problems, you fix one element and apply two pointers on the remainder — O(n²) total.

**Common pitfall.** The array must be sorted (or exhibit some monotone property). Applying two pointers to an unsorted array breaks the invariant and produces wrong answers. Also beware of skipping duplicates in three-sum — after finding a valid triplet, advance both pointers past all equal elements to avoid duplicate output.

sections.title: Pattern 2: Sliding Window
sections.content:
**What it is.** Sliding Window maintains a contiguous subrange `[left, right]` within an array or string, expanding by advancing `right` and shrinking by advancing `left`, without ever re-scanning the interior.

**Recognition signals.** Longest or shortest **contiguous subarray or substring** satisfying a constraint: maximum sum, at most k distinct characters, no repeating characters, contains all characters of a pattern, sum equals a target with positive numbers.

**Fixed-size vs. variable-size windows.** When the window size k is fixed (e.g., "maximum sum of exactly k elements"), simply slide: subtract the outgoing element and add the incoming one in O(1) per step. When the size is variable (e.g., "longest substring with at most 2 distinct chars"), expand `right` freely and shrink `left` only when the constraint is violated.

**Why it is O(n).** Each element crosses the right boundary exactly once and the left boundary at most once — two touches total. No element is ever scanned a third time. This is the key insight: naive re-scanning would cost O(n) per window position for O(n²) overall; the window avoids that by maintaining state incrementally.

**State management.** The window usually carries a frequency map or a running sum. When the map has too many distinct keys, shrink left and decrement the outgoing key's count; remove it from the map when the count hits zero. This bookkeeping is O(1) per pointer move because hash-map operations are amortized constant.

**Common pitfall.** Sliding window breaks on arrays with negative numbers when searching for the maximum sum of a variable-length subarray — negative elements mean shrinking the window is not always correct, and Kadane's algorithm is needed instead. Always check whether values can be negative before reaching for this pattern.

sections.title: Pattern 3: Fast / Slow Pointers
sections.content:
**What it is.** Two pointers traverse a linked list at different speeds: `slow` advances one node per step, `fast` advances two. If the list contains a cycle, fast eventually laps slow inside the loop and they meet. If there is no cycle, fast falls off the end (hits `null`) before they meet.

**Recognition signals.** Linked list cycle detection; finding the **middle node** of a linked list in one pass; finding the **entry point** of a cycle (Floyd's algorithm phase 2); checking if a linked list is a palindrome (find middle, reverse second half, compare).

**Why they always meet inside a cycle.** Suppose the cycle has length C and, at the moment slow enters the cycle, fast is k steps ahead of slow inside the cycle. Each step, fast gains one step on slow (2 − 1 = 1). So they meet after C − k additional steps. Meeting is inevitable and takes at most O(C) extra steps after slow enters the cycle.

**Finding the cycle entry.** After detecting the meeting point, reset one pointer to `head` and advance both at speed 1. They meet exactly at the cycle's entry. The mathematical proof: if the distance from head to the entry is F, and the distance within the cycle from entry to meeting point is a, then at the meeting point the slow pointer has traveled F + a steps, and fast has traveled 2(F + a) = F + a + n*C for some integer n. Solving gives F = n*C − a, which means starting from head and from the meeting point at the same speed, both pointers arrive at the entry simultaneously.

**Complexity.** O(n) time, O(1) space — no hash set needed.

**Common pitfall.** Always check `fast && fast.next` before advancing fast; skipping this check causes a null-pointer error when the list has an odd number of nodes.

sections.title: Pattern 4: Merge Intervals
sections.content:
**What it is.** Given a list of intervals, sort by start time, then sweep through once, greedily merging each interval into the previous one if they overlap.

**Recognition signals.** Merge overlapping intervals; insert a new interval and re-merge; find the minimum number of meeting rooms required; find all free time slots given a list of busy intervals.

**The greedy sweep.** After sorting, maintain a `last` interval being built. For each new interval `[s, e]`: if `s <= last.end`, the intervals overlap — extend `last.end` to `max(last.end, e)`. Otherwise, there is a gap — push `last` to results and start a new interval. Note the `max` on `last.end`: this handles the case where the new interval is fully contained within `last`.

**Why sorting is mandatory.** Without sorted order, the overlap check (`s <= last.end`) is meaningless because a later interval might overlap an earlier one that has already been pushed. Sorting guarantees that if any overlap exists, it involves consecutive intervals in the sorted list.

**Complexity.** O(n log n) due to sorting; the sweep is O(n). Space is O(n) for the output.

**Variant: insert interval.** Given a sorted, non-overlapping list and a new interval, use binary search or a linear scan to find where the new interval fits, then merge. A clean approach is to collect all non-overlapping intervals before the new one, merge everything that overlaps, then append the remainder.

**Common pitfall.** Using `last.end = e` instead of `last.end = Math.max(last.end, e)` will incorrectly shrink the merged interval when a later interval is fully contained within the current one.

sections.caption: Merge intervals: sort once, then a single left-to-right sweep greedily extends or closes each merged interval.

sections.title: Pattern 5: Prefix Sum
sections.content:
**What it is.** Precompute a cumulative sum array `prefix` where `prefix[i]` holds the sum of `arr[0..i-1]`. Then any range sum `arr[l..r]` is `prefix[r+1] - prefix[l]` — constant time after linear preprocessing.

**Recognition signals.** Multiple range-sum queries on an immutable array; count subarrays whose sum equals k; find the equilibrium index; 2D range sum queries (extend to a 2D prefix sum matrix).

**Why the formula works.** `prefix[r+1]` accumulates all elements from index 0 through r. `prefix[l]` accumulates elements 0 through l-1. Their difference cancels the shared prefix, leaving exactly `arr[l] + arr[l+1] + ... + arr[r]`.

**The hash-map trick for subarray sum = k.** A running prefix sum `ps` at index i means the subarray `arr[0..i]` sums to `ps`. If some earlier prefix sum `ps - k` existed at index j, then `arr[j+1..i]` sums to k. Store all prefix sums seen so far in a hash map (value → count). At each step: add `counts.get(ps - k)` to the answer (subarrays ending here with sum k), then record the current `ps` in the map. Initialize with `counts.set(0, 1)` to account for subarrays starting at index 0.

**Complexity.** O(n) preprocessing, O(1) per query. The hash-map variant for subarray counting is O(n) time and space.

**2D extension.** For a matrix, build `prefix[r][c] = sum of all elements in the rectangle (0,0) to (r-1,c-1)`. Then the sum of any sub-rectangle is computable in O(1) using inclusion-exclusion on four prefix values.

**Common pitfall.** Forgetting to initialize `counts.set(0, 1)` in the hash-map variant misses all subarrays that start at index 0 and causes wrong answers silently.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Two Pointers converges in at most n steps — each comparison either returns or permanently eliminates one index. The sliding window uses an index-based seen map so that shrinking left is an O(1) jump rather than a character-by-character crawl. Fast/Slow works by the same logic in both problems: when fast reaches the terminal condition (null or meeting slow), the slow pointer is exactly where we need it.

sections.title: Pattern 6: BFS and DFS
sections.content:
**What they are.** BFS (Breadth-First Search) and DFS (Depth-First Search) are the two fundamental strategies for traversing a graph or tree. BFS explores all nodes at distance d before any node at distance d+1, using a **queue**. DFS follows a path as deep as possible before backtracking, using a **stack** (or the call stack via recursion).

**Recognition signals for BFS.** Shortest path in an unweighted graph; minimum number of steps to reach a target; level-order tree traversal; bipartite graph check; 0/1 BFS on a weighted grid.

**Recognition signals for DFS.** Connected components; island counting in a grid; topological sort (DFS with a finish-time stack); strongly connected components (Tarjan/Kosaraju); cycle detection in directed graphs; path existence; maze exploration.

**Why BFS guarantees shortest path.** BFS visits nodes in non-decreasing order of distance from the source. The first time it reaches the target, no shorter path can exist — any unvisited neighbor is at distance d+1, never at d or less. This guarantee vanishes the moment edge weights are unequal; Dijkstra's algorithm is then needed instead.

**DFS and the recursion/stack duality.** Every recursive DFS call implicitly uses the program's call stack. For very deep graphs (depth 10,000+), this risks stack overflow. An iterative DFS with an explicit stack avoids this and behaves identically, though the traversal order may differ slightly (iterative DFS often reverses the neighbor order relative to recursive DFS).

**Visited tracking.** Always maintain a `visited` set to avoid revisiting nodes in graphs with cycles. Trees (by definition acyclic) do not need it, but adding the check costs nothing and makes code robust if the input turns out to have back-edges.

**Grid problems.** A 2D grid is implicitly a graph where each cell is a node and adjacent (4-directional or 8-directional) cells are edges. DFS flood-fill marks an entire island by mutating the grid (`grid[r][c] = '0'`) to serve as the visited marker, avoiding a separate set. BFS on a grid computes the minimum distance from a source cell to every other cell — standard for problems like 'shortest path in a maze'.

**Complexity.** Both BFS and DFS run in O(V + E) where V is the number of vertices and E the number of edges. For an m×n grid, V = m*n and E ≈ 4*m*n, so O(m*n) overall.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A["Source node S"]
    A --> B["BFS queue: [S]\nvisited: {S}"]
    B --> C["Dequeue S\nEnqueue neighbors A, B"]
    C --> D["Dequeue A\nEnqueue neighbor C"]
    D --> E["Dequeue B\nEnqueue neighbor D"]
    E --> F["Dequeue C → target found\ndistance = 2 hops"]
sections.caption: BFS processes nodes level by level. When C (the target) is first dequeued, the distance 2 is guaranteed to be optimal — no shorter path to C exists.

sections.title: Pattern 7: Backtracking
sections.content:
**What it is.** Backtracking is a recursive, depth-first enumeration that builds a solution incrementally — one choice at a time — and **abandons (prunes) a partial solution** the moment it violates a constraint, instead of continuing to a full solution and discarding it.

**Recognition signals.** Generate all subsets; generate all permutations; generate all combinations summing to a target; generate valid parentheses; solve N-Queens; solve Sudoku; word search in a grid.

**The choose-explore-unchoose template.** Every backtracking function follows the same three-step body: (1) **choose** — add a candidate to the current partial solution; (2) **explore** — recurse with the updated state; (3) **unchoose** — remove the candidate, restoring state for the next iteration. The `unchoose` (undo) step is what distinguishes backtracking from naive recursion: without it, state leaks across branches and produces incorrect results.

**Pruning is the performance lever.** A pruning condition checks whether the current partial solution can possibly be extended to a valid complete solution. If not, skip the recursive call entirely. For example, in combination-sum problems, if the current running sum already exceeds the target, no future additions (all positive) can fix it — prune immediately. Pruning transforms worst-case exponential complexity into something tractable for typical inputs.

**Permutations vs. subsets.** For subsets, you pass a `start` index so each recursive call only considers elements at or after `start` — this prevents re-using elements in different orders. For permutations, you swap elements in-place (choosing which goes in position i) and swap back (unchoose). For combinations with duplicates, sort first and skip duplicate values at the same recursion level with `if (i > start && nums[i] === nums[i-1]) continue`.

**Complexity.** Subsets: O(2^n * n) — 2^n subsets, each copied in O(n). Permutations: O(n! * n). These are worst-case bounds; effective pruning often reduces actual runtime dramatically. Backtracking is the right tool when the constraint space is irregular and cannot be captured by a closed-form combinatorial formula.

**Common pitfall.** Forgetting to push a **copy** of the current array into results — pushing the reference means all result entries will reflect the final (empty) state of the array after backtracking completes.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A["subsets([1,2,3])\nstart=0, cur=[]"] --> B["choose 1\nstart=1, cur=[1]"]
    B --> C["choose 2\nstart=2, cur=[1,2]"]
    C --> D["choose 3 → push [1,2,3]\nunchoose 3"]
    C --> E["push [1,2], unchoose 2"]
    B --> F["choose 3 → push [1,3]\nunchoose 3, unchoose 1"]
    A --> G["choose 2\ncur=[2] ..."]
    A --> H["choose 3\ncur=[3] ..."]
sections.caption: Backtracking decision tree for subsets: each branch chooses an element, recurses, then unchooses (pops) it before trying the next option. The result array collects every state where push is called.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The prefix-sum hash map is the trickiest pattern here. The key insight: `prefix - k` is the sum we need to have seen earlier. The `counts.set(0, 1)` seed handles subarrays that start at index 0 (their prefix was 0 before any element was added). The merge-intervals `Math.max` guard handles containment: if [2,8] is followed by [3,5], the 5 must not shrink the merged end back from 8 to 5. BFS uses a `[node, distance]` tuple so distance is naturally propagated without a separate distance map.

sections.label: Concept
sections.explanation: Islands DFS mutates the grid as its visited set — elegant, O(1) overhead, but destructive. If preservation matters, use a separate Set of 'r,c' strings. Subsets backtracking uses a `start` index so [1,2] and [2,1] are not both generated — order is not restarted. Permutations use in-place swapping so no extra array is needed; swapping back restores the array for the next iteration at the parent level.

sections.content: **A brief history.** Two Pointers and Sliding Window formalized in competitive programming in the 1990s. Floyd's cycle detection was published in Robert Floyd's 1967 Stanford technical report (though the algorithm appeared in D. Knuth's TAOCP as early as 1969). Edsger Dijkstra published the interval-merging idea as part of his analysis of scheduling algorithms around 1970. Prefix sums are as old as numerical analysis itself — Blaise Pascal used equivalent cumulative tables in the 1600s. BFS was formalized by Konrad Zuse in 1945 and popularized by Moore (1959) and Lee (1961) for circuit routing. Backtracking traces to D.H. Lehmer's work on combinatorics in the 1950s.

**Interview execution advice.** Before writing any code: read the problem, identify the recognition signal, name the pattern aloud, and state the complexity. Interviewers reward pattern recognition far more than raw coding speed. Common mistakes to avoid: (1) applying Two Pointers on an unsorted array; (2) forgetting `Math.max` when merging a contained interval; (3) missing `counts.set(0, 1)` in prefix-sum subarray counting; (4) pushing an array reference rather than a copy in backtracking; (5) using DFS when the problem asks for **shortest** path — that requires BFS. Practice labelling 30–40 problems by pattern before practicing solutions; pattern-first training ingrains the reflex that makes interviews feel routine.

items: **Two Pointers** eliminates O(n²) pair-search by exploiting sorted order — converge from both ends, eliminate one candidate per step, O(n) time O(1) space.
**Sliding Window** handles contiguous subarray/substring problems by expanding `right` and shrinking `left` — each element is touched at most twice, guaranteeing O(n) regardless of window size.
**Fast/Slow Pointers** detects cycles and finds midpoints with O(1) space — the hare inevitably laps the tortoise inside any cycle, proven by the speed-difference invariant.
**Merge Intervals** requires sorting by start first; the greedy sweep then merges in a single O(n) pass, always using `Math.max` on the end to handle containment correctly.
**Prefix Sum** enables O(1) range queries after O(n) setup; the hash-map variant counts subarrays summing to k in O(n) — always seed the map with `{0: 1}` to handle subarrays starting at index 0.
**BFS** guarantees shortest path in unweighted graphs by visiting nodes level by level; **DFS** is preferred for connectivity, topological sort, and exhaustive grid exploration.
**Backtracking** is choose-explore-unchoose; the `pop()` (undo) step is mandatory to prevent state leaking across branches, and pruning before recursing is what makes it efficient in practice.

quiz.question: A problem gives you a sorted array and asks for two indices whose values sum to a target. Which pattern solves this in O(n) time and O(1) space?
options: Sliding Window
Two Pointers
Prefix Sum with a hash map
Backtracking
quiz.explanation: Two Pointers is canonical for pair-sum in a sorted array. Initialize left=0 and right=n-1. If the sum is too large, decrement right; if too small, increment left. Sorted order guarantees each step permanently eliminates one candidate, giving O(n) time.

quiz.question: Why does the Sliding Window technique guarantee O(n) time even when the window size varies?
options: It uses binary search to find the optimal window boundaries.
Each element crosses the right boundary once and the left boundary at most once — two touches total.
The window size is always bounded by a constant k.
It stores a prefix sum so that window sums are computed in O(1).
quiz.explanation: The right pointer only advances forward and the left pointer only advances forward. Each element enters the window (right passes it) exactly once and exits (left passes it) at most once, for a total of at most 2n pointer moves — O(n) overall regardless of window size variation.

quiz.question: In Floyd's cycle detection (Fast/Slow Pointers), what mathematical property guarantees the two pointers always meet inside a cycle?
options: The fast pointer always stays exactly 2 nodes ahead of slow, so they cannot pass each other.
Inside a cycle of length C, fast closes the gap by exactly 1 node per step, so they meet within at most C additional steps.
The slow pointer marks visited nodes so fast can find it directly.
Both pointers are reset to the head once fast reaches the tail.
quiz.explanation: Fast moves 2 steps, slow moves 1, so fast gains 1 on slow each iteration. Once both are inside the cycle of length C, the gap closes by 1 per step and reaches 0 within C steps — meeting is inevitable. Outside a cycle, fast hits null first and no meeting occurs.

quiz.question: Why must you use `Math.max(last.end, end)` rather than just `last.end = end` when merging intervals?
options: To sort the output intervals in ascending order of end time.
To handle the case where the incoming interval is fully contained within the current merged interval.
To avoid comparing intervals with negative start times.
Because the intervals may not be sorted by start time yet.
quiz.explanation: If [1,10] is followed by [3,5], the incoming interval is fully contained. Simply assigning last.end = 5 would incorrectly shrink the merged interval from 10 to 5. Math.max(10, 5) = 10 correctly preserves the wider boundary.

quiz.question: In the prefix-sum hash-map approach for counting subarrays summing to k, why must you initialize the map with `{0: 1}` before processing any elements?
options: To avoid a division-by-zero error when prefix equals k at the first element.
To count subarrays that start at index 0 — their needed prior prefix is 0, which must already exist in the map.
To handle arrays containing negative numbers correctly.
To ensure the map is never empty when doing lookups.
quiz.explanation: When the running prefix sum equals k at index i, the subarray arr[0..i] is a valid answer. The lookup checks how many times prefix-k=0 appeared before. Without seeding {0:1}, that lookup returns undefined (treated as 0), silently missing all subarrays starting at index 0.

quiz.question: A problem asks for the shortest number of steps to transform word A into word B by changing one character at a time (word ladder). Which traversal is most appropriate?
options: DFS with memoization
BFS on the implicit word graph
Backtracking with pruning
Two Pointers on the sorted word list
quiz.explanation: BFS guarantees the shortest path in an unweighted graph. Each word is a node; an edge connects two words differing by exactly one character. BFS explores words at edit distance 1 before edit distance 2, so the first time it reaches the target word, that distance is optimal.

quiz.question: In a backtracking solution for generating all subsets, what is the critical purpose of `current.pop()` after the recursive call returns?
options: It removes duplicate elements from the result array.
It terminates the recursion when the subset reaches target size.
It restores the `current` array to its pre-choice state so that the next candidate starts from a clean slate.
It prunes branches that exceed the target sum.
quiz.explanation: Backtracking is choose-explore-unchoose. After exploring all subsets that include nums[i], pop() removes it, restoring `current` to its state before that choice. Without this undo step, subsequent loop iterations inherit nums[i] in `current`, corrupting all future subsets.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT a valid recognition signal for using the Sliding Window pattern?
options: Longest substring with at most k distinct characters.
Minimum size subarray with sum greater than or equal to target.
Shortest path between two nodes in a weighted graph.
Maximum sum of exactly k consecutive elements.
quiz.explanation: Shortest path in a weighted graph is a Dijkstra (or Bellman-Ford) problem, not Sliding Window. The other three — constrained substring length, minimum contiguous subarray by sum, and fixed-size window sum — are all classic Sliding Window applications.

quiz.question: Given `prefix[i] = prefix[i-1] + arr[i-1]` (1-indexed prefix, `prefix[0] = 0`), what is the sum of `arr[l..r]` (0-indexed, inclusive)?
options: prefix[r] - prefix[l]
prefix[r+1] - prefix[l]
prefix[r] - prefix[l-1]
prefix[r+1] - prefix[l+1]
quiz.explanation: prefix[r+1] accumulates arr[0] through arr[r]. prefix[l] accumulates arr[0] through arr[l-1]. Their difference cancels the shared prefix [0..l-1], leaving exactly arr[l] + arr[l+1] + ... + arr[r].

quiz.question: Counting connected components (islands) in a 2D grid of '1's and '0's is most naturally solved by which approach?
options: Two Pointers scanning rows and columns simultaneously.
Prefix Sum over a 2D matrix.
DFS or BFS flood-fill from each unvisited land cell.
Merge Intervals applied to each row independently.
quiz.explanation: Each island is a connected component of '1' cells. DFS (or BFS) from an unvisited '1' cell floods the entire island by marking cells visited, then increments the counter. The outer double loop finds the next unvisited '1' to start the next flood-fill. This visits each cell at most once — O(m*n) total.
